message.content: I heard, then, that around Naucratis of Egypt there came to be one of the old gods there, whose also the bird is sacred, which indeed they call Ibis; and his name, the daimon's itself, was Theuth. This one first found number and calculation and geometry and astronomy, and further draughts and dice, and indeed letters. And Thamus then being king of all Egypt around the great city of the upper place, which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god Ammon, Theuth, having come to this one, displayed the arts, and said they must be handed out to the other Egyptians. But he asked what benefit each has, and as he went through them, as he seemed to speak well or not well, he blamed one thing and praised another. Many things indeed about each art, on both sides, Thamus is said to have declared to Theuth, which it would be a long account to go through. But when it came to letters, "This, O king, the learning," said Theuth, "will provide the Egyptians wiser and more mindful; for a remedy of memory and wisdom was found." But he said: "O most artful Theuth, one man is able to beget the things of art, but another to judge what share of harm and benefit it has for those who are going to use it. And now you, being father of letters, through good will have said the opposite of what it can do. For this will provide forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn, through neglect of memory, inasmuch as through trust in writing they are reminded from outside by alien marks, not from inside themselves by themselves. So not of memory but of reminding you found a remedy. And of wisdom you provide to the students opinion, not truth. For having become hearers of many things by you without teaching, they will seem to be knowers of many things, being, for the most part, without knowledge, and hard to be with, having become seeming-wise instead of wise."

Continuing the translation, I'm working through the Theuth/Thamus myth: Theuth discovering number, calculation, geometry, astronomy, games, and letters; presenting these arts to King Thamus for distribution to the Egyptians; Thamus questioning the benefit of each and judging them one by one; and finally the exchange about writing, where Theuth claims it will make the Egyptians wiser and improve memory, and Thamus begins his famous reply distinguishing the inventor of an art from the judge of its use.

I'm making sure to render the genitive absolute "Θαμοῦ... βασιλεύοντος" literally as "Thamus then being king of all Egypt," keeping the geographic references to the great city and the god Ammon intact as the king's attributes. Then I continue into Thamus's rebuttal: writing will produce forgetfulness since people will rely on external marks rather than their own internal memory, so what Theuth has found is a remedy for reminding, not for memory itself; and as for wisdom, students will gain only the appearance of knowledge without real understanding, becoming seeming-wise rather than truly wise.
